The statement of principles adopted on 26 June 1955 at the Congress of the People in Kliptown, near Johannesburg, by thousands of delegates opposed to apartheid. It opens with the claim that South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white.

It was drawn up by the Congress Alliance: the African National Congress with Indian, Coloured and white democratic groups. Volunteers had gathered demands from people across the country. The charter called for votes for all, equal rights, land shared among those who work it, and the nation's wealth returned to the people. Police broke up the meeting on its second day.

The government saw the charter as treason. In 1956 it arrested 156 leaders, including Nelson Mandela, in the Treason Trial, which ended in 1961 with every one acquitted. Africanists who rejected its non-racial vision left the ANC in 1959 and formed the Pan Africanist Congress. Many of its ideals went into South Africa's constitution of 1996.
